The government isn't shutting down, at least not yet. Late Friday night, just hours before the midnight deadline, the Senate passed a stopgap spending bill, sixty votes to thirty-eight. It keeps the government funded at current levels through January thirtieth, and it includes twelve billion dollars in disaster aid for areas hit by this fall's hurricanes. The White House says President Ellis will sign it on Saturday.

The vote didn't split neatly by party. Eleven Republicans voted yes, while thirty-six Republicans and two Democrats, Paul Grant of Oregon and Lena Brooks of Vermont, voted no.

Hardly anyone sounded thrilled. Majority Leader John Doe said it isn't a bill any of them would have written, but it keeps the lights on while talks continue, and a holiday shutdown would have hurt millions of families. Senator Mary Roe of Utah, who led opposition from the right, called it another kick of the can that adds to the debt. The two Democrats who voted no wanted it to extend child care subsidies that expire at the end of the year.

The disaster money is its own argument. Some Democrats from hurricane-hit states, including Senator Ana Torres of Florida, called twelve billion a down payment, not a recovery plan, since governors had asked for thirty-eight billion. Torres voted yes anyway.

Left-leaning coverage zeroed in on what the bill leaves out, like hurricane aid and child care help, while right-leaning outlets focused on the debt and the missing border security money.

So the clock resets. Congress still needs a full-year funding deal, and the new deadline is the end of January.
